section_1.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
section_1.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
section_1.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
section_2.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

section_3.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
section_3.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
section_3.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

section_4.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
section_4.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
section_4.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

section_5.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
section_5.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
section_5.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

section_6.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
section_6.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
section_6.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

section_7.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
section_7.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
section_7.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

section_8.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
section_8.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
section_8.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

section_1.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
section_1.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
section_1.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
section_2.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

section_3.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
section_3.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
section_3.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

section_4.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
section_4.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
section_4.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

section_5.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
section_5.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
section_5.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

section_6.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
section_6.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
section_6.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

section_7.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
section_7.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
section_7.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

section_8.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
section_8.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
section_8.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

storyboard.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
lecture_lines: Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic.
Build a bridge toward structured scientific prediction.
Ensure sample size is at least thirty.
The results will always follow a bell curve.
Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order.
animations: Show a chaotic mix of shapes on the left and a Bell Curve on the right.
Draw a solid white (#FFFFFF) bridge connecting the two sides.
Display the steps '1. Any Data', '2. n ≥ 30', '3. Normal Shape' along the bridge.
The entire scene glows as the text 'Order from Chaos' appears above.
The bridge and labels fade out, leaving a single golden (#FFD700) Bell Curve.

section_1.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
section_1.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
section_1.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
section_2.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

section_3.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
section_3.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
section_3.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

section_4.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
section_4.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
section_4.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

section_5.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
section_5.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
section_5.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

section_6.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
section_6.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
section_6.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

section_7.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
section_7.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
section_7.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

section_8.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
section_8.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
section_8.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

outline.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
outline.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
outline.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

lecture_lines: Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: The population includes every individual in a group.
We select a sample to measure and label.
Scaling up the sample allows for detailed analysis.
animations: Display a large cloud of small white (#FFFFFF) dots representing the population.
Draw a green (#00FF00) circle around a small group of dots.
Label the cloud 'Population (μ)' and the circle 'Sample (x̄)' in their respective colors.
Scale up the green circle until it fills the screen, showing the sampled dots clearly.
Fade out the population cloud, leaving only the sample dots and the label 'x̄'.

section_3.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
lecture_lines: We calculate the average weight of squirrel groups.
Each sample mean becomes a single data point.
Repeating this process creates a new data distribution.
animations: Show a group of 10 grey (#808080) squares representing individual squirrels.
Calculate their average and display the number above a blue (#0000FF) dot.
The blue dot falls vertically onto a horizontal axis at the bottom.
Repeat the process 5 times, with new dots falling and stacking on the axis.
Speed up the process until dots are falling continuously from above.

section_4.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
lecture_lines: Watch as sample means begin to pile up.
A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form.
This is the birth of the Normal Distribution.
animations: Show the horizontal axis with a growing pile of blue (#0000FF) dots from section 3.
The dots pile up into vertical bars, forming a rough, jagged histogram.
As the number of dots reaches 1,000, the histogram bars smooth out.
Overlay a glowing white (#FFFFFF) Normal Distribution curve over the histogram.
The curve flashes once to emphasize its perfect symmetric shape.

section_5.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
lecture_lines: Small samples often result in messy distributions.
Increasing the sample size fills the power meter.
Reliability is reached once n reaches thirty.
animations: Show a jagged, non-normal histogram in red (#FF0000) with the label 'n = 2'.
Display a vertical 'Power Meter' on the right that is low and red (#FF0000).
Change the label to 'n = 30' and animate the meter filling up to green (#00FF00).
The red histogram transforms into a smooth green (#00FF00) Bell Curve.
Highlight the 'n = 30' text with a yellow (#FFFF00) pulse effect.

section_6.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
lecture_lines: The curve stays centered on the population mean.
We calculate variation using the Standard Error formula.
Small samples produce a wider, flatter bell curve.
Larger samples provide much higher statistical certainty.
Precision increases with the square root of n.
animations: Display the formula 'μ_x̄ = μ' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Display 'Standard Error: σ_x̄ = σ / √n' below it in white.
Show a wide, flat Bell Curve in blue (#0000FF) representing n=30.
Animate the curve becoming taller and narrower as 'n' increases to 1000.
Highlight the '√n' in the formula with yellow (#FFFF00) as the curve narrows.

section_7.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
lecture_lines: We monitor candy bars on a factory line.
Sample means must fall within safe bell limits.
This guarantees consistent quality for every batch.
animations: Show a row of orange (#FFA500) rectangles representing candy bars on a belt.
A blue (#0000FF) scanning line moves across the bars from left to right.
A Bell Curve appears above, with a green (#00FF00) shaded region for 'Safe Limits'.
A single dot (the batch average) falls into the green region.
Fade in the text 'Quality Guaranteed' in green (#00FF00) at the center.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Fetching storyboard data
        title_text = "Introduction: The Hidden Pattern"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.",
            "This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.",
            "A hidden order emerges when we group data.",
            "The peak represents the most common sample mean.",
            "This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors for matching animation elements
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_CURVE = "#0000FF"
        COLOR_PEAK = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_CLT = "#FFFFFF"
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_HIST))
        
        # Create a chaotic, bimodal histogram
        bar_heights = [1.2, 2.5, 1.0, 0.4, 0.6, 2.2, 2.8, 1.4]
        histogram = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=0.4, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=COLOR_HIST, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in bar_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        self.place_in_area(histogram, "B1", "E6")
        self.play(Create(histogram))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        )
        
        chaos_text = Text("CHAOS", font_size=36, weight=BOLD, color=COLOR_CHAOS)
        # Position chaos_text above the histogram
        self.place_in_area(chaos_text, "A1", "A6")
        
        self.play(Write(chaos_text))
        self.play(Indicate(chaos_text, color=COLOR_HIST))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_CURVE)
        )
        
        # Create a smooth blue Bell Curve (Normal Distribution approximation)
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=5, y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        ).hide()
        
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color=COLOR_CURVE, x_range=[-2.5, 2.5])
        curve_group = VGroup(curve)
        self.place_in_area(curve_group, "B1", "E6")
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(chaos_text),
            ReplacementTransform(histogram, curve_group)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(COLOR_PEAK)
        )
        
        # Highlight the peak of the Bell Curve with a yellow vertical line
        peak_top = curve_group.get_top()
        # The bottom of the curve is determined by its lowest points
        peak_bottom = np.array([peak_top[0], curve_group.get_bottom()[1], 0])
        peak_line = Line(
            start=peak_top,
            end=peak_bottom,
            color=COLOR_PEAK,
            stroke_width=5
        )
        
        self.play(Create(peak_line))
        self.play(Flash(peak_line, color=COLOR_PEAK))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(COLOR_CLT)
        )
        
        clt_text = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=32, color=COLOR_CLT)
        # Position CLT text below the curve
        self.place_in_area(clt_text, "F1", "F6")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(clt_text))
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Reset color and finish
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

            "Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.",
            "This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.",
            "A hidden order emerges when we group data.",
            "The peak represents the most common sample mean.",
            "This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors for matching animation elements
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_CURVE = "#0000FF"

            "Small samples often result in messy distributions.",
            "Increasing the sample size fills the power meter.",
            "Reliability is reached once n reaches thirty."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_str, lines_str)
        
        # Define Colors
        RED_COLOR = "#FF0000"
        GREEN_COLOR = "#00FF00"
        YELLOW_COLOR = "#FFFF00"

        bars_red = VGroup(*[

                width=0.2, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=RED_COLOR, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in jagged_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)

        # Position relative to frame bottom
        meter_fill.move_to(meter_frame.get_bottom(), aligned_edge=DOWN).shift(UP * 0.1)

        # Updater for power meter fill bar
        def update_meter(m):
            val = n_tracker.get_value()
            # Linear mapping from n=[2, 30] to height=[0.2, 2.8]
            target_h = interpolate(0.2, 2.8, (val - 2) / 28)
            m.stretch_to_fit_height(target_h)
            m.move_to(meter_frame.get_bottom(), aligned_edge=DOWN).shift(UP * 0.1)
            # Color transition logic
            if val < 30:
                m.set_color(RED_COLOR)
            else:
                m.set_color(GREEN_COLOR)

        meter_fill.add_updater(update_meter)

        self.play(
            Create(bars_red),
            Write(label_n),
            Create(meter_frame),
            FadeIn(meter_fill)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Highlight second lecture line
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN_COLOR))

        label_n_30.move_to(label_n.get_center())

        # Animate sample size increase and power meter fill
        self.play(
            n_tracker.animate.set_value(30),
            Transform(label_n, label_n_30),
            run_time=2.5,
            rate_func=linear
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Highlight third lecture line
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW_COLOR))

        # Smooth Green Bell Curve (Normal Distribution)
        bell_curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([t, 1.8 * np.exp(-t**2), 0]),
            t_range=[-2, 2],
            color=GREEN_COLOR,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        # Positioning bell curve within the same area as the histogram
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve, "B1", "D4")

        # Transform jagged histogram to smooth bell curve
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(bars_red, bell_curve),
            label_n.animate.set_color(YELLOW_COLOR)
        )

        # Pulse effect for the 'Magic Number' n = 30
        self.play(
            Indicate(label_n, color=YELLOW_COLOR, scale_factor=1.4),
            Flash(label_n, color=YELLOW_COLOR, line_length=0.3)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        ]

            )
            
            # Dot falls and stacks
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            self.play(
                new_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos),
                FadeOut(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                run_time=0.6
            )

        # Speed up the process (Continuous dots falling)
        fast_dots_animations = []
        for i in range(40):
            # Sampling from a normal-like distribution for visual effect
            rand_x = random.gauss(self.grid["D3"][0], 0.8)
            # Clamp to axis bounds

            fast_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.06)

            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)

            )
            self.add(fast_dot)
            fast_dots_animations.append(anim)

        self.play(AnimationGroup(*fast_dots_animations))

        def get_stack_pos(x_val):
            bin_idx = int((x_val - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
            count = bin_counts.get(bin_idx, 0)
            bin_counts[bin_idx] = count + 1
            return np.array([self.grid["F1"][0] + bin_idx * bin_width + bin_width/2, self.grid["F1"][1] + 0.1 + count * 0.12, 0])

            new_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.08)
            new_dot.move_to([rand_x, self.grid["D3"][1], 0])
            
            self.play(FadeIn(temp_sq, run_time=0.2), FadeIn(new_dot, run_time=0.2))
            
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            self.play(
                new_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos),
                FadeOut(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                run_time=0.6
            )

        fast_dots_animations = []
        for i in range(40):
            rand_x = random.gauss(self.grid["D3"][0], 0.8)
            rand_x = max(self.grid["F1"][0] + 0.2, min(self.grid["F6"][0] - 0.2, rand_x))
            
            fast_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.06)
            start_pos = np.array([rand_x, 3.5, 0])
            fast_dot.move_to(start_pos)
            
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            delay = i * 0.05
            anim = Succession(
                Wait(delay),
                fast_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos).set_run_time(0.2)
            )
            self.add(fast_dot)
            fast_dots_animations.append(anim)

        self.play(AnimationGroup(*fast_dots_animations))
        self.wait(3)

        # The curve stays centered on the population mean.
        # Display the formula 'μ_x̄ = μ' in white (#FFFFFF)
        self.lecture[0].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW)
        formula_mean = MathTex(r"\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula_mean, 'A3', scale_factor=1.2)
        
        self.play(Write(formula_mean))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # We calculate variation using the Standard Error formula.
        # Display 'Standard Error: σ_x̄ = σ / √n' below it in white.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW)
        
        # Use tex_to_color_map to identify the \sqrt{n} part for later highlighting
        formula_se = MathTex(
            r"\text{Standard Error: } \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}",
            tex_to_color_map={r"\sqrt{n}": WHITE},
            color=WHITE
        )
        self.place_at_grid(formula_se, 'B3', scale_factor=0.9)
        
        self.play(Write(formula_se))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Small samples produce a wider, flatter bell curve.
        # Show a wide, flat Bell Curve in blue (#0000FF) representing n=30.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW)
        
        # Setup Axes in the area D1 to F6
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3, 1],
            y_range=[0, 2, 0.5],
            x_length=5,
            y_length=2.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": WHITE}

        self.place_in_area(axes, 'D1', 'F6', scale_factor=0.8)

        # n value tracker starting at 30
        n_tracker = ValueTracker(30)
        
        # Display n value next to the axes
        n_label_prefix = Text("n = ", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        n_val_disp = DecimalNumber(30, num_decimal_places=0, font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        n_label_group = VGroup(n_label_prefix, n_val_disp).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)

        n_val_disp.add_updater(lambda d: d.set_value(n_tracker.get_value()))

        def get_bell_curve_func():
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            # Parameters scaled for visual clarity:

            amp = 0.3 * np.sqrt(n_val / 30)
            stdev_sq = 30 / n_val
            return axes.plot(

            )

        self.lecture[3].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW)

            n_tracker.animate.set_value(1000),
            run_time=4,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===

        # Highlight the '√n' in the formula with yellow (#FFFF00) as the curve narrows.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW)
        
        # Target the \sqrt{n} sub-mobject
        sqrt_n_part = formula_se.get_part_by_tex(r"\sqrt{n}")
        
        self.play(
            sqrt_n_part.animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW),
            Flash(sqrt_n_part, color=HIGHLIGHT_YELLOW, run_time=1)
        )
        self.wait(3)
        
        # Final cleanup: reset lecture line color
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")

        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

section_1.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
section_1.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
section_1.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
section_2.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

section_3.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
section_3.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
section_3.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

section_4.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
section_4.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
section_4.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

section_5.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
section_5.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
section_5.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

section_6.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
section_6.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
section_6.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

section_7.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
section_7.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
section_7.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

section_8.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
section_8.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
section_8.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Fetching storyboard data
        title_text = "Introduction: The Hidden Pattern"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.",
            "This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.",
            "A hidden order emerges when we group data.",
            "The peak represents the most common sample mean.",
            "This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors for matching animation elements
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_CURVE = "#0000FF"
        COLOR_PEAK = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_CLT = "#FFFFFF"
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_HIST))
        
        # Create a chaotic, bimodal histogram
        bar_heights = [1.2, 2.5, 1.0, 0.4, 0.6, 2.2, 2.8, 1.4]
        histogram = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=0.4, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=COLOR_HIST, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in bar_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        self.place_in_area(histogram, "B1", "E6")
        self.play(Create(histogram))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        )
        
        chaos_text = Text("CHAOS", font_size=36, weight=BOLD, color=COLOR_CHAOS)
        # Position chaos_text above the histogram
        self.place_in_area(chaos_text, "A1", "A6")
        
        self.play(Write(chaos_text))
        self.play(Indicate(chaos_text, color=COLOR_HIST))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_CURVE)
        )
        
        # Create a smooth blue Bell Curve (Normal Distribution approximation)
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=5, y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        )
        
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color=COLOR_CURVE, x_range=[-2.5, 2.5])
        curve_group = VGroup(curve)
        self.place_in_area(curve_group, "B1", "E6")
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(chaos_text),
            ReplacementTransform(histogram, curve_group)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(COLOR_PEAK)
        )
        
        # Highlight the peak of the Bell Curve with a yellow vertical line
        peak_top = curve_group.get_top()
        # The bottom of the curve is determined by its lowest points
        peak_bottom = np.array([peak_top[0], curve_group.get_bottom()[1], 0])
        peak_line = Line(
            start=peak_top,
            end=peak_bottom,
            color=COLOR_PEAK,
            stroke_width=5
        )
        
        self.play(Create(peak_line))
        self.play(Flash(peak_line, color=COLOR_PEAK))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(COLOR_CLT)
        )
        
        clt_text = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=32, color=COLOR_CLT)
        # Position CLT text below the curve
        self.place_in_area(clt_text, "F1", "F6")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(clt_text))
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Reset color and finish
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        # Title and Lecture Lines

        lecture_lines = [
            "The population includes every individual in a group.",
            "We select a sample to measure and label.",
            "Scaling up the sample allows for detailed analysis."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        pop_color = "#FFFFFF"

        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A3", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(pop_dots), Write(pop_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw a green (#00FF00) circle around a group of dots and label them 'Population (μ)' and 'Sample (x̄)'.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Sample selection
        sample_center = self.grid["D4"]

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup data from storyboard
        title_text = "The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels"
        lecture_lines = [
            "We calculate the average weight of squirrel groups.",
            "Each sample mean becomes a single data point.",
            "Repeating this process creates a new data distribution."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors from storyboard
        GREY_COLOR = "#808080"
        BLUE_COLOR = "#0000FF"
        
        # Static elements: Axis at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"], self.grid["F6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Mean Weight", font_size=16, color=WHITE).next_to(axis, DOWN, buff=0.2)
        self.add(axis, axis_label)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Color line 1 to match elements (Grey)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(GREY_COLOR))
        
        # 10 grey squares representing individual squirrels
        squirrels = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.2, color=GREY_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.8) for _ in range(10)])
        squirrels.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.1)
        self.place_in_area(squirrels, "B2", "C5")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(squirrels))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Calculate average and display number above a blue dot
        avg_val = 502
        avg_label = Text(f"{avg_val}g", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        sample_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_dot, "D3")
        avg_label.next_to(sample_dot, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            Write(avg_label),
            FadeIn(sample_dot)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color line 2 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # The blue dot falls vertically onto the axis
        # Vertical fall from D3 to F3
        target_x = self.grid["D3"][0]
        target_y = self.grid["F3"][1] + 0.1
        
        self.play(
            sample_dot.animate.move_to([target_x, target_y, 0]),
            FadeOut(avg_label),
            FadeOut(squirrels),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color line 3 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # Stacking logic setup
        bin_counts = {}
        bin_width = 0.3
        
        def get_stack_pos(x_val):
            # Map x_val to a bin index based on the axis range
            bin_idx = int((x_val - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
            count = bin_counts.get(bin_idx, 0)
            bin_counts[bin_idx] = count + 1
            # Stack dots upwards from the axis
            return np.array([self.grid["F1"][0] + bin_idx * bin_width + bin_width/2, self.grid["F1"][1] + 0.1 + count * 0.12, 0])

        # Register the first dot in the bins
        first_bin_idx = int((target_x - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
        bin_counts[first_bin_idx] = 1

        # Repeat the process 5 times
        for _ in range(5):
            # Flash squirrel group
            temp_sq = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.12, color=GREY_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.6) for _ in range(10)])
            temp_sq.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.05)
            self.place_in_area(temp_sq, "B2", "C5")
            
            # Generate a new sample mean dot
            rand_x = self.grid["D3"][0] + random.uniform(-1.5, 1.5)
            new_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.08)
            new_dot.move_to([rand_x, self.grid["D3"][1], 0])
            
            self.play(
                FadeIn(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                FadeIn(new_dot, run_time=0.2)
            )
            
            # Dot falls and stacks
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            self.play(
                new_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos),
                FadeOut(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                run_time=0.6
            )

        # Speed up the process (Continuous dots falling)
        fast_dots_animations = []
        for i in range(40):
            # Sampling from a normal-like distribution for visual effect
            rand_x = random.gauss(self.grid["D3"][0], 0.8)
            # Clamp to axis bounds
            rand_x = max(self.grid["F1"][0] + 0.2, min(self.grid["F6"][0] - 0.2, rand_x))
            
            fast_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.06)
            # Start falling from above (off-grid Row A)
            start_pos = np.array([rand_x, 3.5, 0])
            fast_dot.move_to(start_pos)
            
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            
            # Create a sequence: wait then move
            delay = i * 0.05
            anim = Succession(
                Wait(delay),
                fast_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos).set_run_time(0.2)
            )
            self.add(fast_dot)
            fast_dots_animations.append(anim)

        self.play(AnimationGroup(*fast_dots_animations))
        self.wait(3)

    def construct(self):
        # Initialize layout
        self.setup_layout("The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell", [
            "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up.",
            "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form.",
            "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        ])
        
        # Define hex colors
        BLUE_HEX = "#0000FF"
        WHITE_HEX = "#FFFFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Lecture: "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Create horizontal axis on grid row F
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"], self.grid["F6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Means", font_size=16, color=WHITE)
        # Position label near axis (within 1 grid unit)
        self.place_at_grid(axis_label, "F3", scale_factor=1.0)
        axis_label.shift(DOWN * 0.5)
        
        self.add(axis, axis_label)
        
        # Create bars to represent piling dots
        bars = VGroup()
        for i in range(1, 7):
            # Initial tiny bar
            bar = Rectangle(
                width=0.6, 
                height=0.01, 
                fill_color=BLUE_HEX, 
                fill_opacity=0.7, 
                stroke_width=1, 
                stroke_color=BLUE_HEX
            )
            # Center bar horizontally at grid column i, vertically at Row F
            self.place_at_grid(bar, f"F{i}")
            bars.add(bar)
        
        self.add(bars)
        
        # Grow bars into a jagged distribution
        rough_heights = [0.4, 2.2, 1.8, 3.1, 1.2, 0.6]
        self.play(
            *[bar.animate.stretch_to_fit_height(h, about_edge=DOWN) for bar, h in zip(bars, rough_heights)],
            run_time=2.5,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Lecture: "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form."
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Smooth into symmetric bell heights
        smooth_heights = [0.6, 2.0, 3.5, 3.5, 2.0, 0.6]
        self.play(
            *[bar.animate.stretch_to_fit_height(h, about_edge=DOWN) for bar, h in zip(bars, smooth_heights)],
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Lecture: "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE_HEX))
        
        # Create the ideal Normal Distribution curve
        def normal_pdf_func(x):
            # Symmetric curve peaking at 3.5
            return 3.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 0.8)**2)
            
        curve = FunctionGraph(
            normal_pdf_func,
            x_range=[-2.5, 2.5],
            color=WHITE_HEX,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        
        # Align curve with the axis and bars
        # Grid center for Row F is between F3 and F4
        dist_center = (self.grid["F3"] + self.grid["F4"]) / 2
        curve.move_to(dist_center, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        # Add glow effect
        glow = curve.copy().set_stroke(width=12, opacity=0.3, color=WHITE_HEX)
        
        # Animate curve creation
        self.play(Create(curve), FadeIn(glow), run_time=2)
        
        # Flash animation to emphasize shape
        self.play(
            curve.animate.set_stroke(width=8), 
            glow.animate.set_stroke(width=20, opacity=0.5), 
            run_time=0.4
        )
        self.play(
            curve.animate.set_stroke(width=4), 
            glow.animate.set_stroke(width=12, opacity=0.3), 
            run_time=0.4
        )
        
        self.wait(2)

            "Reliability is reached once n reaches thirty."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_str, lines_str)
        
        # Define Colors
        RED_COLOR = "#FF0000"
        GREEN_COLOR = "#00FF00"
        YELLOW_COLOR = "#FFFF00"

        jagged_heights = [0.6, 1.4, 0.4, 1.1, 0.3, 1.5, 0.7, 1.2, 0.2, 0.8]
        bars_red = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=0.2, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=RED_COLOR, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in jagged_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_in_area(bars_red, "B1", "D4")
        
        # Label: n = 2
        label_n = Text("n = 2", font_size=24, color=RED_COLOR)
        self.place_at_grid(label_n, "A2")

        self.place_in_area(meter_frame, "B5", "E5")

        # Meter fill (initial low red state)

        # Position relative to frame bottom
        meter_fill.move_to(meter_frame.get_bottom(), aligned_edge=DOWN).shift(UP * 0.1)

        # Updater for power meter fill bar
        def update_meter(m):
            val = n_tracker.get_value()
            # Linear mapping from n=[2, 30] to height=[0.2, 2.8]
            target_h = interpolate(0.2, 2.8, (val - 2) / 28)
            m.stretch_to_fit_height(target_h)
            m.move_to(meter_frame.get_bottom(), aligned_edge=DOWN).shift(UP * 0.1)
            # Color transition logic
            if val < 30:
                m.set_color(RED_COLOR)
            else:
                m.set_color(GREEN_COLOR)

        meter_fill.add_updater(update_meter)

        self.play(
            Create(bars_red),
            Write(label_n),
            Create(meter_frame),
            FadeIn(meter_fill)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        label_n_30.move_to(label_n.get_center())

        # Animate sample size increase and power meter fill
        self.play(

            Transform(label_n, label_n_30),
            run_time=2.5,
            rate_func=linear
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW_COLOR))

        # Smooth Green Bell Curve (Normal Distribution)
        bell_curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([t, 1.8 * np.exp(-t**2), 0]),
            t_range=[-2, 2],
            color=GREEN_COLOR,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        # Positioning bell curve within the same area as the histogram
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve, "B1", "D4")

        # Transform jagged histogram to smooth bell curve
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(bars_red, bell_curve),
            label_n.animate.set_color(YELLOW_COLOR)
        )

        # Pulse effect for the 'Magic Number' n = 30
        self.play(
            Indicate(label_n, color=YELLOW_COLOR, scale_factor=1.4),
            Flash(label_n, color=YELLOW_COLOR, line_length=0.3)
        )
        self.wait(2)

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section7Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "Real-World Application: Quality Control",
            [
                "We monitor candy bars on a factory line.",
                "Sample means must fall within safe bell limits.",
                "This guarantees consistent quality for every batch."
            ]
        )

        # Colors
        ORANGE_C = "#FFA500"
        BLUE_C = "#0000FF"
        GREEN_C = "#00FF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(ORANGE_C)
        
        # Create a row of orange rectangles (candy bars)
        candy_bars = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(width=0.4, height=0.2, color=ORANGE_C, fill_opacity=0.8, fill_color=ORANGE_C)
            for _ in range(6)
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        self.place_in_area(candy_bars, "E1", "E6")
        
        # Scanner line
        scanner_line = Line(
            start=candy_bars.get_left() + UP * 0.4,
            end=candy_bars.get_left() + DOWN * 0.4,
            color=BLUE_C,
            stroke_width=6
        )
        
        self.play(Create(candy_bars))
        self.add(scanner_line)
        self.play(scanner_line.animate.move_to(candy_bars.get_right()), run_time=2)
        self.play(FadeOut(scanner_line))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(GREEN_C)
        
        # Bell Curve
        curve_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 0.5],
            axis_config={"include_tip": False},
            x_length=4, y_length=2
        )
        
        def normal_pdf(x):
            return np.exp(-x**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)
        
        bell_curve = curve_axes.plot(normal_pdf, color=WHITE)
        shaded_region = curve_axes.get_area(bell_curve, x_range=[-1, 1], color=GREEN_C, opacity=0.3)
        
        # Group axes and plots
        curve_group = VGroup(curve_axes, bell_curve, shaded_region)
        self.place_in_area(curve_group, "B1", "D6")
        
        label_safe = Text("Safe Limits", font_size=16, color=GREEN_C)
        self.place_in_area(label_safe, "D3", "D4", scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(Create(bell_curve))
        self.play(FadeIn(shaded_region), FadeIn(label_safe))
        
        # A single dot (batch average) falls into the limits
        dot = Dot(color=WHITE)
        # Position it inside the bell curve center hump
        dot_pos = curve_axes.c2p(0, 0.2)
        dot.move_to(dot_pos)
        self.play(FadeIn(dot, shift=DOWN))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN_C)
        
        quality_text = Text("Quality Guaranteed", font_size=24, color=GREEN_C)
        self.place_in_area(quality_text, "F1", "F6", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(Write(quality_text))
        self.wait(2)

import numpy as np
import random

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):

        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):

class Section8Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Initializing Layout
        self.setup_layout(
            "Summary: The Bridge to Statistics",
            [
                "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic.",
                "Build a bridge toward structured scientific prediction.",
                "Ensure sample size is at least thirty.",
                "The results will always follow a bell curve.",
                "Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order."
            ]
        )

        # Colors for mapping lines to animations
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FF5555"
        COLOR_BRIDGE = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_STEPS = "#55AAFF"
        COLOR_NORMAL = "#FFD700"
        COLOR_ORDER = "#00FFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic."
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        
        # Chaos Group: Random primitive shapes
        chaos_elements = VGroup()
        for _ in range(15):
            # Using random.choice instead of np.random.choice to avoid array dimension issues with Mobjects
            shape = random.choice([
                Circle(radius=0.1, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Square(side_length=0.2, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Triangle(color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6).scale(0.12)
            ])
            # Spread shapes around a relative center
            shape.shift(np.random.uniform(-0.7, 0.7, 3))
            chaos_elements.add(shape)
        
        self.place_in_area(chaos_elements, "B1", "D2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Faint bell curve on the right representing the goal
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 0.5], 
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "stroke_width": 1},
            tips=False
        ).set_color(GRAY)
        bell_curve_plot = axes.plot(lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 2), color=COLOR_NORMAL, stroke_opacity=0.3)
        bell_group = VGroup(axes, bell_curve_plot)
        self.place_in_area(bell_group, "B5", "D6", scale_factor=0.6)

        self.play(Create(chaos_elements), FadeIn(bell_group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Build a bridge toward structured scientific prediction."
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_BRIDGE)
        
        # Bridge connecting Chaos (C1) and Structure (C6)
        bridge = Line(self.grid["C1"], self.grid["C6"], color=COLOR_BRIDGE, stroke_width=6)
        self.play(Create(bridge))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "Ensure sample size is at least thirty."
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_STEPS)
        
        step1 = Text("1. Any Data", font_size=20, color=COLOR_STEPS)
        step2 = Text("2. n \u2265 30", font_size=20, color=COLOR_STEPS)
        step3 = Text("3. Normal Shape", font_size=20, color=COLOR_STEPS)
        
        self.place_at_grid(step1, "D1", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(step2, "D3", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(step3, "D5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Write(step1))
        self.play(Write(step2))
        self.play(Write(step3))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # "The results will always follow a bell curve."
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_NORMAL)
        
        # Transform faint bell curve into a clear golden one
        clear_bell_plot = axes.plot(lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 2), color=COLOR_NORMAL, stroke_width=4)
        self.play(
            Transform(bell_curve_plot, clear_bell_plot),
            axes.animate.set_color(COLOR_NORMAL).set_stroke(opacity=1.0),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order."
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_ORDER)
        
        order_text = Text("Order from Chaos", font_size=28, color=COLOR_ORDER)
        self.place_at_grid(order_text, "A3", scale_factor=1.1)
        
        # Glow effect for order_text
        glow = order_text.copy().set_stroke(width=10, opacity=0.3).set_color(COLOR_ORDER)
        
        self.play(Write(order_text), FadeIn(glow))
        self.wait(1.5)
        
        # Final visual: Clear Golden Bell Curve central to the universe
        final_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 0.5], 
            axis_config={"include_tip": False},
            tips=False
        ).set_color(COLOR_NORMAL)
        final_plot = final_axes.plot(lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 2), color=COLOR_NORMAL, stroke_width=6)
        final_bell_group = VGroup(final_axes, final_plot)
        self.place_in_area(final_bell_group, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=1.4)

        self.play(
            FadeOut(chaos_elements),
            FadeOut(bridge),
            FadeOut(step1), FadeOut(step2), FadeOut(step3),
            FadeOut(order_text), FadeOut(glow),
            Transform(bell_group, final_bell_group),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(3)

    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2

        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Title and Lecture Lines
        title_text = "Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample"
        lecture_lines = [
            "The population includes every individual in a group.",
            "We select a sample to measure and label.",
            "Scaling up the sample allows for detailed analysis."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        pop_color = "#FFFFFF"
        sample_color = "#00FF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a large cloud of small white (#FFFFFF) dots representing the population.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Population cloud
        np.random.seed(42)
        pop_dots = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.04, color=pop_color) for _ in range(120)])
        
        # Scatter them in area B2 to E5
        for dot in pop_dots:
            dot.move_to(np.array([
                np.random.uniform(1.0, 5.0),
                np.random.uniform(-2.2, 1.8),
                0
            ]))
            
        # Using Text instead of MathTex to avoid LaTeX dependency error
        pop_label = Text("Population (μ)", color=pop_color)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A3", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(pop_dots), Write(pop_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw a green (#00FF00) circle around a group of dots and label them 'Population (μ)' and 'Sample (x̄)'.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Sample selection
        sample_center = self.grid["D4"]
        sample_circle = Circle(radius=0.8, color=sample_color, stroke_width=4)
        sample_circle.move_to(sample_center)
        
        # Using Text instead of MathTex to avoid LaTeX dependency error
        sample_label = Text("Sample (x̄)", color=sample_color)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, "F4", scale_factor=0.6)

        # Distinguish dots: some dots turn green to indicate they are in the sample
        dots_inside = VGroup()
        dots_outside = VGroup()
        for dot in pop_dots:
            if np.linalg.norm(dot.get_center() - sample_center) < 0.8:
                dot.set_color(sample_color)
                dots_inside.add(dot)
            else:
                dots_outside.add(dot)
        
        # Ensure enough dots are inside for visual clarity
        if len(dots_inside) < 10:
            for _ in range(10 - len(dots_inside)):
                offset = np.random.uniform(-0.6, 0.6, size=3)
                offset[2] = 0
                d = Dot(radius=0.04, color=sample_color).move_to(sample_center + offset)
                dots_inside.add(d)
                pop_dots.add(d)

        self.play(Create(sample_circle))
        self.play(Write(sample_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Scale up the green circle until it fills the screen, showing the sampled dots clearly.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Scaling and focus
        target_pos = self.grid["C3"]
        
        # We group sample elements to scale together
        sample_view = VGroup(sample_circle, dots_inside, sample_label)
        
        # We fade out everything else to focus on the sample
        self.play(
            FadeOut(dots_outside),
            FadeOut(pop_label),
            sample_view.animate.scale(2.5).move_to(target_pos),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Final state
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(1)

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Fetching storyboard data
        title_text = "Introduction: The Hidden Pattern"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.",
            "This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.",
            "A hidden order emerges when we group data.",
            "The peak represents the most common sample mean.",
            "This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors for matching animation elements
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_CURVE = "#0000FF"
        COLOR_PEAK = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_CLT = "#FFFFFF"
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_HIST))
        
        # Create a chaotic, bimodal histogram
        bar_heights = [1.2, 2.5, 1.0, 0.4, 0.6, 2.2, 2.8, 1.4]
        histogram = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=0.4, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=COLOR_HIST, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in bar_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        self.place_in_area(histogram, "B1", "E6")
        self.play(Create(histogram))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        )
        
        chaos_text = Text("CHAOS", font_size=36, weight=BOLD, color=COLOR_CHAOS)
        # Position chaos_text above the histogram
        self.place_in_area(chaos_text, "A1", "A6")
        
        self.play(Write(chaos_text))
        self.play(Indicate(chaos_text, color=COLOR_HIST))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_CURVE)
        )
        
        # Create a smooth blue Bell Curve (Normal Distribution approximation)
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=5, y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        )
        
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color=COLOR_CURVE, x_range=[-2.5, 2.5])
        curve_group = VGroup(curve)
        self.place_in_area(curve_group, "B1", "E6")
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(chaos_text),
            ReplacementTransform(histogram, curve_group)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(COLOR_PEAK)
        )
        
        # Highlight the peak of the Bell Curve with a yellow vertical line
        peak_top = curve_group.get_top()
        # The bottom of the curve is determined by its lowest points
        peak_bottom = np.array([peak_top[0], curve_group.get_bottom()[1], 0])
        peak_line = Line(
            start=peak_top,
            end=peak_bottom,
            color=COLOR_PEAK,
            stroke_width=5
        )
        
        self.play(Create(peak_line))
        self.play(Flash(peak_line, color=COLOR_PEAK))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(COLOR_CLT)
        )
        
        clt_text = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=32, color=COLOR_CLT)
        # Position CLT text below the curve
        self.place_in_area(clt_text, "F1", "F6")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(clt_text))
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Reset color and finish
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

class Section8Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Initializing Layout
        self.setup_layout(
            "Summary: The Bridge to Statistics",
            [
                "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic.",
                "Build a bridge toward structured scientific prediction.",
                "Ensure sample size is at least thirty.",
                "The results will always follow a bell curve.",
                "Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order."
            ]
        )

        # Colors for mapping lines to animations
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FF5555"
        COLOR_BRIDGE = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_STEPS = "#55AAFF"
        COLOR_NORMAL = "#FFD700"
        COLOR_ORDER = "#00FFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic."
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        
        # Chaos Group: Random primitive shapes
        chaos_elements = VGroup()
        for _ in range(15):
            # Using random.choice instead of np.random.choice to avoid array dimension issues with Mobjects
            shape = random.choice([
                Circle(radius=0.1, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Square(side_length=0.2, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Triangle(color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6).scale(0.12)
            ])
            # Spread shapes around a relative center
            shape.shift(np.random.uniform(-0.7, 0.7, 3))
            chaos_elements.add(shape)
        
        self.place_in_area(chaos_elements, "B1", "D2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Faint bell curve on the right representing the goal
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 0.5], 
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "stroke_width": 1},
            tips=False
